question.text: Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 2x+3y+z=1 \\ 6x-2y-z=-14 \\ 3x+y-z=1 \end{cases} \] Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $27,$ then $z=$
question.explanation:
First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

\[ \begin{cases} {\color{blue}2}x + {\color{blue}3}y + {\color{blue}1}z = {\color{red}1} \\ {\color{blue}6}x + ({\color{blue}-2})y+ ({\color{blue}-1})z = {\color{red}-14} \\ {\color{blue}3}x + {\color{blue}1}y + ({\color{blue}-1})z = {\color{red}1}. \end{cases} \]

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}2 & \color{blue}3 & \color{blue}1 \\ \color{blue}6 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{blue}3 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-1 \end{matrix}\right| = 27. \end{align}

Now, to find $D_z$, we replace the third column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

\begin{align} D_z = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}2 & \color{blue}3 & \color{red}1 \\ \color{blue}6 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{red}-14 \\ \color{blue}3 & \color{blue}1 & \color{red}1 \end{matrix}\right| &= 2 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} -2 & -14 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - 3 \cdot\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -14 \\ 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + 1 \cdot\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = 2(-2 + 14) - 3(6 + 42) + (6 + 6) \\[5pt] & = 24 - 144 + 12 \\[5pt] & = -108. \end{align}

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

\begin{align} z & = \dfrac {D_z} D = \dfrac {-108} {27} = -4. \end{align}

question.text: Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 2x+y-z=1 \\ x-2y+2z=3 \\ 3x-2y+z=2 \end{cases} \] Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $5,$ then $x=$
question.explanation:
First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

\[ \begin{cases} {\color{blue}2}x + {\color{blue}1}y + ({\color{blue}-1})z = {\color{red}1} \\ {\color{blue}1}x + ({\color{blue}-2})y+ {\color{blue}2}z = {\color{red}3} \\ {\color{blue}3}x + ({\color{blue}-2})y + {\color{blue}1}z = {\color{red}2}. \end{cases} \]

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}2 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}2 \\ \color{blue}3 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix}\right| = 5. \end{align}

Now, to find $D_x$, we replace the first column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{red}1 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{red}3 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}2 \\ \color{red}2 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix}\right| &= 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + (-1) \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = (-2 - (-4)) - (3 - 4) - (-6 - (-4)) \\[5pt] & = 2 + 1 + 2 \\[5pt] & = 5. \end{align}

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

\begin{align} x & = \dfrac {D_x} D = \dfrac {5} {5} = 1. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

\[ \begin{cases} 5x - 3y + z = 5 \\ x + y -2 z = -3 \\ -5x + 4 z = -1 \end{cases} \]

Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $7,$ then $y=$
question.explanation:
First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

\[ \begin{cases} {\color{blue}5}x + ({\color{blue}-3})y + {\color{blue}1}z = {\color{red}5} \\ {\color{blue}1}x + {\color{blue}1}y + ({\color{blue}-2})z = {\color{red}-3} \\ {\color{blue}-5}x + {\color{blue}0}y + {\color{blue}4} z = {\color{red}-1} \end{cases} \]

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}5 & \color{blue}-3 & \color{blue}1\\ \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-2\\ \color{blue}-5 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}4 \end{matrix}\right| = 7 \end{align}

Now, to find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the second column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

\begin{align} D_y = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}5 & \color{red}5 & \color{blue}1\\ \color{blue}1 & -\color{red}3 & \color{blue}-2\\ \color{blue}-5 & \color{red}-1 & \color{blue}4 \end{matrix}\right| & = 5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -3 & -2 \\ -1 & 4 \end{matrix}\right| -5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 4 \end{matrix}\right| + 1 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -3 \\ -5 & -1 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = 5(-12 - 2) - 5 (4 - 10) + (-1 - 15)\\[5pt] & = -70 + 30 - 16 \\[5pt] & = -56. \end{align}

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

\begin{align} y & = \dfrac {D_y} D = \dfrac {-56} 7 = -8. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

\[ \begin{cases} x + y + 3z = -2 \\ 2x - y = 3 \\ -x - 2y + z = 6 \end{cases} \]

Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $-18,$ then $x=$
question.explanation:
First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

\[ \begin{cases} {\color{blue}1}x + {\color{blue}1}y + {\color{blue}3}z = {\color{red}-2} \\ {\color{blue}2}x + ({\color{blue}-1})y+ {\color{blue}0}z = {\color{red}3} \\ ({\color{blue}-1})x + ({\color{blue}-2})y + {\color{blue}1}z = {\color{red}6}. \end{cases} \]

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}3 \\ \color{blue}2 & \color{blue}-1 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{blue}-1 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix}\right| = -18. \end{align}

Now, to find $D_x$, we replace the first column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{red}-2 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}3 \\ \color{red}3 & \color{blue}-1 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{red}6 & \color{blue}-2 & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix}\right| &= -2 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| -1 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 3 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| + (-1) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] & = -2(-1 - 0) - (3 - 0) - (-6+6) \\[5pt] & = 2 -3 - 0 \\[5pt] & = -1. \end{align}

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

\begin{align} x & = \dfrac {D_x} D = \dfrac {-1} {-18} = \dfrac{1}{18}. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

\[ \begin{cases} 3x + 5y - z = 1 \\ 2x - 3z = -2 \\ -x + y - 2z = 6 \end{cases} \]

Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $42,$ then $x=$
question.explanation:
First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

\[ \begin{cases} {\color{blue}3}x + {\color{blue}5}y + ({\color{blue}-1})z = {\color{red}1} \\ {\color{blue}2}x + {\color{blue}0}y+ ({\color{blue}-3})z = {\color{red}-2} \\ ({\color{blue}-1})x + {\color{blue}1}y + ({\color{blue}-2})z = {\color{red}6}. \end{cases} \]

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{blue}3 & \color{blue}5 & \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{blue}2 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}-3 \\ \color{blue}-1 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-2 \end{matrix}\right| = 42. \end{align}

Now, to find $D_x$, we replace the first column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} \color{red}1 & \color{blue}5 & \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{red}-2 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}-3 \\ \color{red}6 & \color{blue}1 & \color{blue}-2 \end{matrix}\right| &= 1 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 0 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 \end{matrix}\right| -5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -2 & -3 \\ 6 & -2 \end{matrix}\right| + (-1) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -2 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] & = (0 + 3) - 5(4 + 18) - (-2-0) \\[5pt] & = 3 -110 + 2 \\[5pt] & = -105. \end{align}

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

\begin{align} x & = \dfrac {D_x} D = \dfrac {-105} {42} = -\dfrac 5 2. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 2x + 3y + 2z = k \\ x + y = -1 \\ y + z = 2 \end{cases} \]

Given that $y=-5$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $1,$ find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
First, let's write the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} 2 & 3 & 2\\ 1 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| = 1 \end{align}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y = \dfrac{D_y}{D},$ where

\begin{align} D_y = \left|\begin{matrix} 2 & k & 2\\ 1 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| & = 2 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| - k \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right| + 2 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = 2(-1 - 0) - k(1 - 0) + 2(2-0) \\[5pt] & = -2 - k + 4 \\[5pt] & = 2-k. \end{align}

Therefore, we have

\[ y = \dfrac{D_y}{D} = \dfrac{2-k}{1}=2-k. \]

From the problem statement, we know that $y=-5.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

\begin{align} 2-k & = -5 \\[5pt] k & = 7. \end{align}

question.text: Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} kx + 2y - 4z = -4 \\ x -2 y + 5z = -6 \\ 10x + y + 2 z = 8. \end{cases} \] Given that $x = -\dfrac{20}{3}$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $12-9k,$ find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} k & 2 & -4\\ 1 & -2 & 5\\ 10 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right| = 12 - 9k \end{align}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x = \dfrac{D_x}{D},$ where

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} -4 & 2 & -4\\ -6 & -2 & 5\\ 8 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right| & = (-4) \cdot\left|\begin{matrix} -2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right| - 2 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -6 & 5 \\ 8 & 2 \end{matrix}\right| +(-4) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -6 & -2 \\ 8 & 1 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = -4(-4 - 5) - 2(-12 -40) - 4(-6+16)\\[5pt] & = 36 + 104 -40 \\[5pt] & = 100. \end{align}

Therefore, we have

\[ x = \dfrac{D_x}{D} = \dfrac{100}{12-9k}. \]

From the problem statement, we know that $x=-\dfrac{20}{3}.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

\begin{align} \dfrac {100}{12 - 9k} & = -\dfrac {20}{3}\\[5pt] 15 & = -12 + 9k\\[5pt] 9k & = 27\\[5pt] k & = 3. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} x - y + 5z = -1 \\ 2x + 3y + 2z = 0 \\ x + 4y = k \end{cases} \]

Given that $x=-4$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $15,$ find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
First, let's write the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -1 & 5\\ 2 & 3 & 2\\ 1 & 4 & 0 \end{matrix}\right| = 15 \end{align}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x = \dfrac{D_x}{D},$ where

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} -1 & -1 & 5\\ 0 & 3 & 2\\ k & 4 & 0 \end{matrix}\right| & = -1 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 \end{matrix}\right| - (-1) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 0 & 2 \\ k & 0 \end{matrix}\right| + 5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 0 & 3 \\ k & 4 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = -(0 - 8) + (0 - 2k) +5(0-3k) \\[5pt] & = 8 - 2k - 15k \\[5pt] & = 8-17k. \end{align}

Therefore, we have

\[ x = \dfrac{D_x}{D} = \dfrac{8-17k}{15}. \]

From the problem statement, we know that $x=-4.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

\begin{align} \dfrac {8-17k}{15} & = -4 \\[5pt] 8-17k & = -60 \\[5pt] -17k & = -68 \\[5pt] k & = 4. \end{align}

question.text: Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 5x-3y-z=1 \\ x+4y+kz=-1 \\ 2x+3y+4z=9. \end{cases} \] Given that $z = 1$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $97 - 21k,$ find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} 5 & -3 & -1\\ 1 & 4 & k\\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{matrix}\right| = 97 - 21k \end{align}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $z$ is given by $z = \dfrac{D_z}{D},$ where

\begin{align} D_z = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1\\ 1 & 4 & -1\\ 2 & 3 & 9 \end{vmatrix} & = 5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 9 \end{matrix}\right| - (-3) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 9 \end{matrix}\right| + 1 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = 5(36 + 3) + 3(9 + 2) + (3-8)\\[5pt] & = 195 + 33 - 5 \\[5pt] & = 223. \end{align}

Therefore, we have

\[ z = \dfrac{D_z}{D} = \dfrac{223}{97 - 21k}. \]

From the problem statement, we know that $z=1.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

\begin{align} \dfrac {223}{97-21k} & = 1\\[5pt] 223 & = 97-21k\\[5pt] 21k & = -126\\[5pt] k & = -6. \end{align}

question.text: Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 6x + 5y - 3z = 2 \\ 4x -5 y + kz = 1 \\ -2x + 10y -5 z = -2. \end{cases} \] Given that $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $160-70k,$ find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

\begin{align} D = \left|\begin{matrix} 6 & 5 & -2\\ 4 & -5 & k\\ -2 & 10 & -5 \end{matrix}\right| = 160-70k \end{align}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x = \dfrac{D_x}{D},$ where

\begin{align} D_x = \left|\begin{matrix} 2 & 5 & -3\\ 1 & -5 & k\\ -2 & 10 & -5 \end{matrix}\right| & = 2 \cdot\left|\begin{matrix} -5 & k \\ 10 & -5 \end{matrix}\right| - 5 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & k \\ -2 & -5 \end{matrix}\right| +(-3) \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 1 & -5 \\ -2 & 10 \end{matrix}\right|\\[5pt] & = 2(25-10k) - 5(-5+2k) - 3(10-10)\\[5pt] & = 50-20k+25-10k+0 \\[5pt] & = 75-30k. \end{align}

Therefore, we have

\[ x = \dfrac{D_x}{D} = \dfrac{75-30k}{160-70k}. \]

From the problem statement, we know that $x=\dfrac{1}{2}.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

\begin{align} \dfrac {75-30k}{160-70k} & = \dfrac {1}{2}\\[5pt] 2(75-30k) & = 160-70k\\[5pt] 150-60k & = 160-70k\\[5pt] 10k & = 10\\[5pt] k &= 1. \end{align}
